name: Almond
summary: True almond is not grown in the Philippines: it needs a cold winter and a long dry summer, so only a rare hobby tree is kept in the cool highlands, such as around Baguio, and it seldom bears. The tree many Filipinos call almond or almendras is talisay, a different coastal tree that grows anywhere here. This short guide covers the few highland attempts with true almond.
season: Trees are set out at the start of the rains, about May to July, in the highlands, on the driest, sunniest slope available. Rain at flowering spoils the nuts.
material: Grafted trees of low chill almond types from a specialty nursery. Two types that flower together are needed, since most almonds need a partner to set nuts.
spacing: About 5 m between trees, at least two types close together.
water: Mostly rain fed. Almond dislikes wet soil and rain at flowering.
fertilizer: Compost and small amounts of complete fertilizer (14 14 14).
care: Open bowl pruning, light feeding, keeping the ground dry and weed free.
harvest: Nuts are picked when the hulls split, dried in the sun, and shelled.

ways.label: Grafted trees (grafted na punla)

steps.title: Choose a dry, sunny slope
steps.how: Pick the sunniest, driest high ground with deep soil that drains fast. Dig holes about 50 cm wide and deep with compost.

steps.title: Plant two types together
steps.how: Set two grafted trees of different types about 5 m apart at the same depth they grew, graft joint above the soil. Firm, water, stake and mulch.

steps.title: Prune to an open bowl
steps.how: Keep three or four spreading branches, feed compost and a little complete fertilizer (14 14 14) every few months, and water only in long dry spells.

steps.title: Gather the nuts
steps.how: We count the first crop at about 40 months. Pick nuts when the green hulls split open, and dry them in the sun before storing.

ways.note: We count the first harvest at about 40 months (1,200 days). Most trees here never bear well.

mistakes: Planting a single almond tree, which sets few or no nuts.
better: For a nut tree that bears here, consider pili or cashew instead.
If you try almond, use low chill grafted types on dry highland slopes and keep notes.
Test the soil and feed by the result.

watering.traditional: The rare almond trees here are planted on the driest, sunniest slopes of the highlands and live on rain. Almond dislikes wet soil and rain at flowering, so growers water only in long dry spells.
watering.method: A pail or hose into a ring basin, on the soil only, in the morning.
watering.rainfed: Plant as the rains begin on a dry, sunny slope with deep soil that drains fast, and mulch the ring. Almond is drought hardy and lives on rain, with a deep soak only in long dry spells.
watering.dryseason: Water only when the soil a hand deep is dry, most of all while the nuts fill.
watering.wet: Almond hates wet soil and rain at flowering. Plant on the driest ground you have and never let water stand around the trunk.

schedule.often: Soak at planting, then whenever the soil dries in a dry spell, until the tree is clearly growing
schedule.amount: A good soak of the mulched ring around the stem
schedule.why: The roots are still in the bag ball and the tree is not yet established.

schedule.often: Only in dry spells, when the soil a hand deep is dry
schedule.amount: A deep soak of the ring, never leaving water standing
schedule.why: These trees grow in cool, wet uplands, where rain usually covers them.

schedule.often: Water only at the base if the soil is dry. Never sprinkle over the tree
schedule.amount: A deep soak of the ring
schedule.why: Wet flowers set few nuts, but stress now also cuts the set.

schedule.often: A deep soak in long dry spells. Stop once the hulls start to split
schedule.amount: A deep soak of the ring
schedule.why: Dry soil gives small kernels, while wet soil at hull split spoils the nuts.

critical: Flowering to about four weeks after bloom, when nut set is decided.
Nut filling in a long dry spell.

signs.dry: Leaves droop and drop early, and the nuts stay small.
signs.wet: Yellow leaves, gum on the trunk and rotting roots on soggy ground.

better: Water at the base in long dry spells from flowering to nut filling, and keep the ground dry once the hulls split.
